rv.q: For 90 largely plotless minutes, theatergoers are riveted to this play, unable to extricate themselves from both the performances and the show itself.
Molina, an actor in constant demand on both sides of the pond, plays Rothko at full titanic force.
As Rothko, the strapping Molina burns up the stage.
What we see, above all, is an artist seeing, and it’s impossible not to feel thrilled by the privilege.
As forcefully delivered in Molina’s volcanic performance, this torrent of observations is consistently engrossing.
The actor inhabits Rothko completely, giving one of those unnerving performances that makes you believe in the possibility of reincarnation.
Alfred Molina is majestic as Rothko, defying the future he reads in the face of Eddie Redmayne, who holds his own as Rothko’s young assistant.
Love, loyalty, honesty, kindness and status are among the values tested by the hard times that Grimm lays out in this resonant, solidly crafted piece, handsomely mounted by Kate Whoriskey.
John Logan's 'Red' is a smart, focused play about the aging Mark Rothko and his young assistant.
Red is a masterpiece of writing, acting and direction that burns with the passion of creation itself.
This is a booming, blustery Molina (who'll be tough to beat come Tony Awards time) as the man whose genius was perhaps outstripped only by the enormity of his ego.
Alfred Molina and Eddie Redmayne deliver powerhouse performances in this absorbing two-character drama
"Red" is a compelling example of how a thinking theater can simultaneously entertain and educate.
The conversation sometimes tilts so close to lecture that you silently wonder, 'Is there a docent in the house?'
There's barely a cliché left unturned in John Logan's 'Red.'
It turns out to be an engrossing look at Abstract Expressionist painter Mark Rothko.
But for a subject so involved and characters so passionate, Red doesn't excite.
